summary: Describes a transport model for SNMP that uses TLS or DTLS, providing authentication and privacy for network management messages. It defines how the TLS Transport Model implements the features of an SNMP transport subsystem. It is an Internet Standard.

eli5.summary: SNMP lets tools check on network equipment. This wraps those questions and answers in an encrypted tunnel, like putting a note in a locked box so nobody can read or change it.

questions: what is tlstm snmp transport model
which port does snmp over tls use
subtitle: How SNMP messages travel inside TLS or DTLS, so network management traffic is authenticated, tamper-proof and private.

tldr.problem: SNMP messages carry sensitive management data and operations, and need a transport that proves who is talking and protects the messages from being altered, replayed or read.
tldr.mechanism: The TLS Transport Model (TLSTM) sends SNMP over TLS on TCP or DTLS on UDP, authenticates both ends with X.509 certificates, and maps the client's certificate to a tmSecurityName that SNMP access control can use.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 5953 and has been updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9456. IANA assigned ports 10161 and 10162 for it.

today: RFC 6353 is an Internet Standard. It obsoletes RFC 5953 and has been updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9456.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 6353 defines the TLS Transport Model (TLSTM) for SNMP. It plugs into the SNMPv3 architecture as a transport model inside the Transport Subsystem, and it uses either TLS for TCP or DTLS, the datagram variant, for UDP. Both rely on X.509 public keying infrastructure. Only certificate-based authentication is covered; other forms are out of scope.

The TLS mode suits large amounts of data over a stream, while the DTLS mode suits environments that prefer a connectionless transport. The RFC uses (D)TLS when a statement applies to both, and calls the two ends of the connection client (opens the connection) and server (listens for it).

The document also defines a MIB module, SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB, for managing the model. It obsoletes RFC 5953; the changes are corrections of editorial errata, updated references (IDNA 2008 in place of IDNA 2003) and updated MIB dates.
sections.eli5: SNMP is a way for tools to ask network gadgets how they are doing. This RFC says how to send those chats through a secret tunnel instead of out in the open.

sections.title: Where TLSTM Fits in SNMP
sections.content:
The TLSTM sits between the (D)TLS layer and the Message Dispatcher of the SNMP engine. When sending, it hands unencrypted, unauthenticated messages from the Dispatcher to (D)TLS to be protected. When receiving, it takes decrypted and integrity-checked messages from (D)TLS and passes them up. It also translates between (D)TLS-specific security parameters and SNMP's model-independent ones.

A session in this RFC is a secure association between two TLS Transport Models, and one session may carry several SNMP messages. The session is the TLSTM's own notion, not the (D)TLS internal session. Each session has a tlstmSessionID, which MUST NOT change for the session's lifetime and MUST uniquely identify it. The (D)TLS internal SessionID is not suitable because it can change, for example during renegotiation.

Per-message transport details, including the authenticated identity, are kept in a cache referenced by tmStateReference. The RFC uses abstract service calls sendMessage() and receiveMessage() between the Dispatcher and the transport model, plus openSession() and closeSession().
sections.eli5: Think of a mail room. The TLSTM puts each letter in a locked pouch before it leaves and unlocks pouches that arrive, then hands the letters to the right desk.

sections.title: Threats and Message Protection
sections.content:
The model addresses the threats named in the SNMP architecture. (D)TLS verifies that messages are not modified in transit, and an implementation MUST support authenticating both server and client to defeat masquerade. Replay and reordering are handled by a Message Authentication Code that includes a sequence number, and DTLS uses a sliding window for replay protection because UDP has no sequencing. Implementations MUST support encryption against eavesdropping.

Denial of service is not required to be solved by an SNMP security protocol, but DTLS over UDP is exposed to spoofed addresses. The DTLS cookie mechanism helps against that, though it gives no defense against attacks from valid addresses.

The architecture's three security levels are noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv and authPriv. The TLSTM MUST ensure the (D)TLS connection gives at least the level the application requested, and the NULL integrity and encryption algorithms MUST NOT be used to satisfy a request for authentication or privacy. Implementations SHOULD allow configuring how algorithms map to SNMPv3 security levels, since algorithms change over time.
sections.eli5: The tunnel stops sneaky people from changing your message, copying an old one, reading it, or pretending to be someone else. It will not let a lock that does nothing count as a real lock.

sections.title: Certificates and Identity
sections.content:
TLSTM implementations are REQUIRED to support X.509 certificates. Entities need certificates, either signed by trusted Certification Authorities or self-signed, plus root certificates for verifying others, and SHOULD have a revocation mechanism. Trusted public keys MUST be installed in the server through a trusted out-of-band mechanism.

When a client certificate arrives, the server derives the tmSecurityName using the snmpTlstmCertToTSNTable. Its mappings include a certificate's subjectAltName or CommonName to a name, or a certificate fingerprint to a directly specified name. Deployments SHOULD map the subjectAltName. The security model, such as the Transport Security Model (TSM), may then turn the tmSecurityName into a securityName for access control.

The tmSecurityName MUST be constant for a session, and messages MUST NOT be sent through a connection established under a different one. The RFC also warns that standard VACM limits securityNames to 32 octets, so a long derived name (its example is a 32-octet name from an IPv6 address plus a TSM prefix, giving 36 octets) will not work with VACM.

Both ends of a connection MUST check the other side's certificate against what is expected, to avoid man-in-the-middle attacks. (D)TLS only shows that a trusted CA signed the certificate; authorization is up to an access control model such as VACM.
sections.eli5: Each side shows an ID card, and each checks the other's card against a list. The name on the card then decides what that visitor is allowed to do.

sections.title: Sessions, Sending and Receiving
sections.content:
(D)TLS MUST negotiate a cipher suite that uses X.509 certificates and MUST authenticate both client and server. Because certificates are checked when the connection opens, renegotiation with different certificates MUST NOT be done; implementations either disable renegotiation (RECOMMENDED) or present the same certificate and verify the other end does too. For DTLS over UDP, each SNMP message MUST fit in a single UDP datagram, the server MUST support DTLS cookies (enabling them by default is RECOMMENDED), and replay protection MUST be used.

Sending. The transport model looks up an existing session matching the transport domain, address, security name and requested level. If none exists it opens one, and if opening fails it discards the message and counts the error.

Opening as a client. The client picks a certificate and cipher suites, runs the (D)TLS handshake and MUST verify the server certificate is the expected one. It MUST NOT send SNMP messages until the server is authenticated, its own certificate has been sent and the connection is fully established. Failures increment counters, and notifications SHOULD be sent for an unknown or invalid server certificate.

Accepting as a server. The server MUST request a certificate from the client and MUST NOT accept SNMP messages until it has been authenticated. Servers that host several principals on one port SHOULD use the Server Name Indication extension.

Closing. Closing MUST include sending a close_notify TLS alert.
sections.eli5: Before any real talking, both sides show their IDs and only then start chatting. When finished, one says a polite goodbye so the other can tidy up.

sections.title: The SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB
sections.content:
The MIB module defines two textual conventions (an address format for (D)TLS connections and a certificate fingerprint), statistical counters, configuration tables and notifications. The counters report session opens, accepts, closes, and the various errors, such as unknown or invalid server certificates.

Three tables matter. The snmpTlstmParamsTable extends the SNMP-TARGET-MIB to say which client certificate to use for a target. The snmpTlstmAddrTable says what server certificate to expect. The snmpTlstmCertToTSNTable maps incoming client certificates to tmSecurityNames, and rows must be searched in order starting with the lowest snmpTlstmCertToTSNID. Two notifications alert managers when a server's certificate was unknown or failed validation.

Because these tables decide who is trusted, changes to them need to be adequately authenticated, and encryption of the SNMP traffic that touches them is highly recommended.
sections.eli5: The MIB is the settings page and the scoreboard: it holds the list of who is allowed in and counts how many visits went wrong.

sections.title: Ports, Operations and Cautions
sections.content:
IANA assigned default ports for command messages and for notifications. Each applies to both TCP (TLS) and UDP (DTLS). It also assigned object identifiers 8 and 9 under snmpDomains for the TLS and DTLS transport domains, and the prefixes tls and dtls.

Operationally, implementations SHOULD close sessions gracefully, SHOULD detect broken sessions (for example with heartbeats) and SHOULD limit session lifetimes. Perfect Forward Secrecy is RECOMMENDED, and SSL 2.0 MUST NOT be requested, offered or used.

Only SNMPv3 messages using the Transport Security Model or another transport-aware security model are RECOMMENDED over TLSTM. SNMPv1 and v2c, and USM, take their identity from the message itself, so using them with a secure transport is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: There are two special doors for these secure chats, one for questions and one for alerts. Use the new-style ID badges, because the old ones ignore the secure door.
